unit.title: Manage personal stress in the workplace

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Some questions are about difficult feelings: if any question upsets you, you may stop and speak to your instructor or the Centre's counsellor. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is stress?
options: A kind of illness that only managers get
A sign that a person is lazy or weak
Something that only happens at home, never at work
The body and mind's reaction to pressure or demands

questions.stem: Which statement about stress is true?
options: All stress is harmful and must be avoided completely
Some pressure helps, but too much for too long is harmful
Stress only affects people who are not good at their jobs
Stress cannot affect the body, only the mind

questions.stem: Which of these is a common physical sign of stress?
options: Headaches, tight muscles and trouble sleeping
Better sleep and more energy than usual
A steady heartbeat and relaxed shoulders
Feeling calm and hungry at regular times

questions.stem: Which is a common behaviour sign that a co-worker may be under too much stress?
options: Arriving on time every day and joking with the team as usual
Taking normal breaks and eating lunch with others
Snapping at people, making mistakes and missing work
Keeping their station clean and their trolley tidy

questions.stem: Which of these is an emotional sign of stress?
options: Feeling cheerful, rested and relaxed for most of the working day
Looking forward to coming to work
Feeling anxious, irritable or low most of the time
Feeling proud when a guest says thank you

questions.stem: Which of these is a common cause of stress at work?
options: Too much work and deadlines that cannot be met
Clear instructions and a fair workload
A supervisor who listens and gives support
Regular breaks and enough rest time between each shift

questions.stem: In a hot, busy hotel kitchen, which conditions can add to a cook's stress?
options: Good extraction fans and cool drinking water
Heat, noise, rushed orders and little space
A clean, well-lit kitchen with a clear order system
Regular breaks away from the stove

questions.stem: Which of these is a cause of stress outside work that can still affect a person at work?
options: Getting enough sleep every night
Spending time with supportive friends
Taking part in a hobby they enjoy
Money worries or family problems

questions.stem: Why can stress be dangerous in a busy kitchen?
options: Stress makes the oven use more gas
A stressed cook may lose focus and get cut or burnt
Stress makes the knives go blunt more quickly
Stressed cooks always work more slowly and safely

questions.stem: If high stress goes on for a long time, what can it lead to?
options: Health problems such as high blood pressure and depression
Stronger muscles and better eyesight
A longer life and fewer illnesses
No effects at all, because the body soon gets fully used to it

questions.stem: What is "burnout"?
options: A burn from hot oil or the handle of a hot pan
An oven fault that comes from being left on too long
Running out of cooking gas in the middle of service
Feeling worn out and drained after long-term stress

questions.stem: What is a stress diary used for?
options: Writing down the hours you have worked so that you are paid
Keeping a list of your co-workers' mistakes
Noting what stressed you, when, and how you reacted
Planning holidays for the whole year

questions.stem: Which of these is a healthy way to cope with stress?
options: Regular exercise, such as walking, dancing or football
Drinking more alcohol after work to relax
Smoking more cigarettes during breaks
Staying up very late every night scrolling on your phone

questions.stem: Why does getting enough sleep help you manage stress?
options: It means you can skip breakfast and lunch
A rested body and mind cope better with pressure
It stops you from ever feeling any stress again at all
It means you do not need to take breaks at work

questions.stem: Working in the Jamaican heat, in a laundry or a kitchen, which simple habit helps both your health and your stress levels?
options: Drinking sweet energy drinks all through the day instead of water
Skipping lunch to finish the job sooner
Working through every break to save time
Drinking enough water and taking short breaks somewhere cool

questions.stem: Which is a quick relaxation method you can use during a short break?
options: Shouting at the nearest person to let off steam
Running up and down the stairs ten times
Slow, deep breathing for a few minutes
Drinking three cups of strong coffee

questions.stem: Why is using alcohol or drugs to cope with stress a bad idea?
options: They are too expensive to buy every week
They hide the problem, harm health and are unsafe at work
They make you too relaxed to enjoy your work
They only work on weekends and holidays

questions.stem: Which of these is an unhealthy way of coping with stress?
options: Cutting yourself off from friends and family
Talking to someone you trust about the problem
Going for a walk at lunchtime
Making a list of tasks in order of importance

questions.stem: How can a "to-do" list help with stress at work?
options: It means you never have to finish any task
It lets someone else do all of your work
It shows what must be done, so you can take it step by step
It replaces any need to talk to your supervisor about the work

questions.stem: You have several tasks and not enough time. What should you do first?
options: Do the easiest tasks first and leave the rest
Try to do every one of the tasks at the same time, quickly
Leave them all and hope they go away
Sort them by how urgent and important they are

questions.stem: Your supervisor asks you to clean an extra villa when you already cannot finish your own rooms before check-in. What is the best response?
options: Explain your workload politely and agree on priorities
Say yes, then skip all your breaks every day to finish it
Refuse rudely and walk away from the supervisor
Say yes but quietly leave the villa undone

questions.stem: What does it mean to be assertive?
options: Always getting your own way by shouting
Saying what you need clearly and calmly, with respect
Agreeing with everyone to avoid arguments
Keeping quiet about problems so you do not upset anyone

questions.stem: A co-worker keeps taking supplies from your housekeeping trolley without asking, and it is making you angry. What is the best first step?
options: Hide their supplies so that they know how it feels
Shout at them in the corridor, in front of the guests
Talk to them calmly in private about the problem
Ignore it and let your anger build up

questions.stem: Who could a trainee at the Centre talk to if stress is affecting their work?
options: Nobody, because stress is a private matter
Only a guest who happens to be staying at the villa during that week
Someone they do not know on social media
Their instructor, the Centre's counsellor or someone they trust

questions.stem: When should a person see a doctor or other health professional about stress?
options: Only after they have been off work sick for a whole year or more
When stress affects sleep, health or daily life for weeks
Never, as doctors do not deal with stress
Only if a co-worker tells them to go

questions.stem: A co-worker tells you they feel hopeless and are thinking of harming themselves. What should you do?
options: Take it seriously, stay with them and get help at once
Tell them to stop being silly and get back to work
Promise to keep it a secret and say nothing to anybody
Tell everyone on the shift so that they all know

questions.stem: What can an employer do to reduce work stress for staff?
options: Give staff more work with shorter deadlines
Stop all breaks so that work finishes sooner
Keep any changes to the work a secret until the very last minute
Plan fair workloads, give clear instructions and listen

questions.stem: What does "work–life balance" mean?
options: Working every day of the week, including holidays
Carrying a tray so that it stays level and does not tip
Having enough time for work, rest, family and interests
Earning the same amount as everyone else

questions.stem: The hotel is changing the shift roster, and you feel worried about it. Which is the most helpful thing to do?
options: Stop coming to work until it changes back
Spread rumours about the change to all the other staff on your shift
Ask the supervisor for the facts and how it affects you
Keep the worry to yourself and say nothing

questions.stem: You notice that a co-worker seems very stressed. What is a helpful thing to do?
options: Tease them a little so that they laugh and forget all about it
Ask quietly if they are OK and listen to them
Tell the rest of the team about their problems
Avoid them until they feel better

questions.stem: Which kind of eating helps the body cope with stress?
options: Regular meals with fruit, vegetables and water
Skipping meals and eating snacks late at night
Mostly sugary drinks and fried food
One very large meal at the end of the day only

questions.stem: Why are regular short breaks important during a long double shift?
options: They are only for people who are not strong enough
They mean the work can be left unfinished
They give time to check social media
They help you rest, stay alert and avoid mistakes

questions.stem: Which way of thinking helps to reduce stress?
options: Expecting every shift to go wrong
Focusing on what you can control
Blaming yourself for every problem
Comparing yourself with everyone else

questions.stem: Why is it useful to know your own early signs of stress?
options: So that you can hide them from your supervisor
So that you can take time off work whenever you feel like it
So that you can blame others for your stress
So that you can act early, before stress builds up

questions.stem: What should a personal stress action plan include?
options: A list of people to blame for your stress
The dates of every public holiday and long weekend for the whole year
The things that stress you, steps to deal with them, and who can help
Only a list of foods that you dislike

questions.stem: A trainee is being bullied by another trainee, and it is causing stress. What should they do?
options: Report it to the instructor or another trusted staff member
Fight back so that the bully stops
Keep quiet and put up with it
Leave the course without telling anyone

questions.stem: How does physical activity help to reduce stress?
options: It makes you too tired to do any work
It means that you no longer need any sleep at night
It only helps if done for five hours a day
It releases tension and improves mood and sleep

questions.stem: Why does talking about a problem with someone you trust often help?
options: It means the problem is now their job to fix, not yours
It can ease the worry and help you see a way forward
It always makes the problem go away at once
It gives you something to complain about later

questions.stem: In the busy tourist season, the hotel is short of staff and shifts are long. Which is the most helpful thing a worker can do?
options: Skip meals and breaks to keep up with the work
Plan rest on days off and tell the supervisor if it is too much
Take every extra shift offered without saying anything
Stop speaking to co-workers until the season ends

questions.stem: Which is a good way to switch off from work stress at home?
options: Spend time on hobbies, family, faith or rest
Check work messages every hour until midnight
Keep going over the day's problems in your head
Argue with family about what went wrong at work

questions.stem: You have tried a new way of coping with stress for two weeks. What should you do next?
options: Give up, because it did not work on the first day
Keep on doing it forever, whether it helps you or not
Tell everyone on the team that they must all use the same method
Check whether it has helped and change your plan if needed

questions.stem: Where can you find out what support your workplace or the Centre offers for stress?
options: In the oven's operating manual or its warranty card
In the handbook, or from student support staff
On the back of the restaurant's menu card
From a stranger on social media

questions.stem: A cook working at the deep fryer feels exhausted and cannot concentrate. What is the safest thing to do?
options: Carry on frying, but work a little faster to finish sooner
Turn the fryer up so that the food cooks more quickly
Make the station safe, tell the supervisor and take a break
Drink an energy drink and keep working

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of "positive" pressure that can help you perform well?
options: A fair deadline that keeps you focused
Being shouted at every day by a co-worker
Working 16-hour shifts every day
Not knowing if you will have a job next week

questions.stem: Who is responsible for managing your own stress?
options: Only your doctor
Only your employer
Nobody, as it cannot be managed
You, with support from others

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Some questions are about difficult feelings: if any question upsets you, you may stop and speak to your instructor or the Centre's counsellor. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What do the letters EAP stand for, in workplace support services?
Name the hormone the body releases quickly when it senses danger, to prepare it for action.
The body's automatic reaction to danger is called "fight or ___". What is the missing word?
What is the word for the things or events that cause a person stress?
Health guides say most adults need at least how many hours of sleep a night?
When setting goals, what does the "S" in SMART stand for?
Stress affects a person's physical health. What other kind of health does it affect? (Two words)
What do the letters HR stand for, as the name of a hotel's staff department?
Health guides commonly suggest adults do at least how many minutes of moderate exercise a week?
What is the word for losing too much water from the body, which makes you tired, irritable and less able to cope in a hot kitchen or laundry?
Name the drug found in coffee, tea and energy drinks that can make anxiety and poor sleep worse if you have too much.
What is the word for being able to bounce back after difficult times?
Name the body system that fights off illness, which long-term stress can weaken.
What do the letters OSH stand for, in workplace safety?
What is the word for deep tiredness and lack of energy that makes it hard to concentrate and work safely on a long shift?

essays.stem: Explain what workplace stress is, and describe the difference between helpful pressure and harmful stress.
essays.modelAnswer: Stress is the way the body and mind react when the demands on a person feel greater than their ability to cope. When we face pressure, the body releases hormones such as adrenaline, so the heart beats faster and the muscles get ready for action. A little pressure can be helpful. For example, a fair deadline to have a villa ready by 3 p.m. check-in can keep a room attendant focused and working well, and the feeling passes once the job is done. This is sometimes called positive pressure. Stress becomes harmful when the pressure is too much, goes on for too long, or the person feels they have no control over it, such as too many rooms every day, constant conflict, rude guests or worry about money. Then the body stays on alert, and the person may become tired, ill, anxious or unable to concentrate. Harmful stress can lead to mistakes, accidents, poor health and burnout, so it should be noticed early and managed.
markingPoints: Stress is the body and mind's reaction when demands feel greater than the ability to cope
Describes the body's reaction (hormones, faster heart, alert)
Helpful pressure: short-term, keeps you focused, passes when the task is done, with an example
Harmful stress: too much, too long or no control, with an example
Effects of harmful stress (illness, mistakes, accidents, burnout) and the need to manage it early

essays.stem: Describe the physical, emotional and behaviour signs of stress. Give at least two examples of each.
essays.modelAnswer: Stress shows itself in the body, in feelings and in the way people act. Physical signs include headaches, a tight neck and shoulders, an upset stomach, a racing heart, feeling tired all the time and trouble sleeping. Some people catch colds more often, because stress weakens the body's defences. Emotional signs include feeling worried or anxious, being irritable or quick to anger, feeling low or tearful, feeling overwhelmed and losing confidence. A stressed person may also find it hard to concentrate, make decisions or remember things. Behaviour signs include snapping at co-workers or guests, arguing, making more mistakes than usual, coming late or missing work, withdrawing from friends, eating much more or much less, and using more alcohol, cigarettes or caffeine. In a hotel, a stressed worker may rush, skip safety steps, forget a guest's request or lose their temper at the front desk. Everyone shows stress in their own way, so it helps to know your own early signs and to notice changes in others.
markingPoints: At least two correct physical signs (such as headaches, tight muscles, poor sleep, upset stomach)
At least two correct emotional signs (such as anxiety, irritability, feeling low or overwhelmed)
At least two correct behaviour signs (such as snapping, mistakes, lateness, withdrawing, more alcohol)
Mentions effects on thinking or concentration
Notes that signs differ between people and links them to safety or service at work

essays.stem: Describe common causes of stress for workers in hotels and villas, both at work and outside work.
essays.modelAnswer: At work, a common cause is too much work in too little time, for example a room attendant with many check-outs to clean before the new guests arrive, or a kitchen with a full restaurant and a banquet on the same night. Long and changing shifts, double shifts and working on weekends and holidays make it hard to rest. In the busy tourist season, properties are often short of staff. Dealing with angry, rude or demanding guests is stressful, especially when the worker must stay polite. Unclear instructions, conflict with co-workers or a supervisor, bullying or feeling unfairly treated add pressure. Working conditions matter too: the heat of a kitchen or laundry, noise, heavy lifting and standing all day make people tired and tense. Worry about losing work in the slow season can also be stressful. Outside work, money problems, family problems, caring for children or sick relatives, long or costly travel to the property, poor housing and health problems can all follow a person into work.
markingPoints: Workload and time pressure (rooms before check-in, busy service)
Long, changing or double shifts and the busy season
Difficult guests, unclear instructions, conflict or bullying
Working conditions such as heat, noise, lifting and standing
Outside work: money, family, travel, housing or health problems

essays.stem: Explain why stress is a safety issue in a hotel kitchen or housekeeping department, and describe what a worker should do if stress is affecting their concentration.
essays.modelAnswer: Hotel kitchens and housekeeping departments have many hazards: sharp knives, hot oil, steam, gas, slicers, cleaning chemicals, wet floors, heavy linen bags and broken glass. Working safely needs full attention. A stressed worker may be tired, distracted or in a hurry, so they are more likely to skip a safety step, forget gloves, mix up chemicals, leave a pan handle sticking out or lift something too heavy alone. This can injure them, a co-worker or a guest, and can lead to poor service. Stress can also cause poor sleep and fatigue, which slow reactions. If stress is affecting their concentration, the worker should stop the task and make it safe, for example by turning off the fryer or putting the chemical away. They should tell the supervisor or instructor honestly that they cannot focus, take a short break, drink water and breathe slowly. If needed, they can ask to change to a lower-risk task for a while. If the problem keeps happening, they should talk to someone about the cause and get support.
markingPoints: Kitchens and housekeeping have serious hazards that need full attention
Stress causes distraction, rushing, fatigue and mistakes
Links this to injury to self, co-workers or guests
Stops and makes the task safe, and tells the supervisor honestly
Takes a break, may change to a lower-risk task, and seeks support if it continues

essays.stem: Describe four healthy ways to manage stress, and explain how each one helps.
essays.modelAnswer: Regular physical activity, such as walking, football, dancing or cycling, helps because it uses up the energy that stress builds up in the body, loosens tight muscles and releases chemicals that improve mood and sleep. Getting enough sleep, usually at least seven hours for an adult, helps because a rested body and mind think more clearly and cope better with pressure. Shift workers can help their sleep by keeping a regular bedtime where they can, and a dark, quiet room. Eating regular, healthy meals and drinking enough water, especially in the heat, keeps energy steady and avoids the tiredness and irritability that come from hunger or dehydration. Talking to someone you trust, such as a friend, family member, instructor, pastor or counsellor, helps because sharing a problem can ease the worry and help you see a way forward. Other good ways include planning your work with a to-do list, taking short breaks, slow deep breathing, and making time for hobbies, faith and family. The best plan uses a few of these together, every day.
markingPoints: First healthy method with a correct explanation (for example exercise)
Second healthy method with a correct explanation (for example sleep)
Third healthy method with a correct explanation (for example healthy eating and water)
Fourth healthy method with a correct explanation (for example talking, planning, breathing, hobbies)
Notes that using several methods regularly works best

essays.stem: Describe how a front desk agent can stay calm and manage their own stress when a guest is angry or rude.
essays.modelAnswer: First, I would remind myself that the guest is usually angry about the problem, not about me, so I should not take it personally. I would keep my voice low and calm, take a slow breath, and keep a relaxed, open posture. I would let the guest speak without interrupting, and listen carefully so that I understand the real problem, for example a room that was not ready at check-in. I would say sorry for the trouble, repeat the main point back so the guest knows I have understood, and explain what I can do and by when. If the guest becomes abusive or threatening, or I cannot solve the problem, I would call my supervisor or security rather than argue. After the guest has gone, I would take a short break if I can, drink some water, and tell my supervisor or a co-worker what happened, so that I do not carry the stress through the rest of the shift.
markingPoints: Does not take it personally and keeps own voice and body calm
Listens without interrupting to understand the problem
Apologises, confirms the problem and explains what can be done
Calls the supervisor or security if the guest is abusive or the problem cannot be solved
Takes a short break or talks it through afterwards to release the stress

essays.stem: Explain how good time management and setting priorities can reduce stress, using examples from a housekeeping or kitchen shift.
essays.modelAnswer: Much work stress comes from feeling that there is too much to do and not enough time. Good time management gives back a feeling of control. At the start of the shift, I can write a to-do list of everything that must be done, for example cleaning four check-out rooms, two stay-over rooms and restocking my trolley. Then I sort the tasks by how urgent and important they are, and do the most urgent and important first, such as the villa for a guest arriving early at noon, or a room marked as a VIP arrival. I break big jobs into smaller steps, so that I can see progress and tick them off. I estimate how long each task will take and leave some spare time for problems. I keep my trolley stocked so that I do not waste trips. If I still cannot fit everything in, I tell my supervisor early and politely, explain my workload and agree which tasks come first. Planning like this reduces rushing, mistakes and last-minute panic.
markingPoints: Links stress to feeling there is too much to do, and time management to control
Uses a to-do list
Sorts tasks by urgency and importance, with a housekeeping or kitchen example
Breaks jobs into steps, estimates time and prepares in advance
Tells the supervisor early and agrees priorities if work cannot fit

essays.stem: Describe how to deal calmly and assertively with a conflict with a co-worker, for example over shared linen, supplies or equipment.
essays.modelAnswer: First, I would wait until I feel calm, rather than reacting in anger, and take a few slow breaths. Then I would ask to speak with the co-worker in private, at a good time, not in a guest corridor or in front of guests. I would explain the problem clearly and calmly, using "I" statements, for example: "I get held up when the clean towels from my trolley go missing, because I have to go back to the linen room." I would not shout, call names or blame. Then I would listen to their side without interrupting, because there may be a reason I did not know about, such as the linen room running short. Together we would look for a fair solution, for example labelling trolleys, asking before taking anything, or telling the supervisor that more linen is needed. We would agree what each of us will do. If the problem continues, or if there is bullying or a threat, I would report it to the supervisor rather than let it build up.
markingPoints: Waits until calm before speaking
Speaks in private at a suitable time, away from guests
States the problem clearly and calmly with "I" statements, without blame
Listens to the other person's side
Agrees a fair solution, and reports to the supervisor if it continues or is serious

essays.stem: Describe where a trainee or hotel worker can get help with stress, and explain when they should seek professional help.
essays.modelAnswer: Help can come from many places. At the Centre, a trainee can talk to their instructor, the guidance counsellor or student support staff, using the support contacts that the Centre gives in its handbook or on its notice board. At work, a worker can talk to their supervisor or the human resources department, and some employers have an employee assistance programme, which gives free, private counselling. Outside work, family, trusted friends, a pastor or church group, or a community group can listen and support. Health professionals, such as a doctor at a health centre, a counsellor or a psychologist, can give advice and treatment. A person should seek professional help when stress lasts for weeks, when it affects their sleep, eating, health or ability to work, when they feel low or hopeless most of the time, or when they are relying on alcohol or drugs to cope. If someone has thoughts of harming themselves, they need help straight away. Do not leave them alone: tell the instructor or the Centre's counsellor, and if they are in immediate danger, call the emergency services or go to the nearest hospital.
markingPoints: Help at the Centre or work: instructor, counsellor, the Centre's support contacts, supervisor, human resources, EAP
Help outside work: family, friends, pastor, community groups
Professional help: doctor, counsellor, psychologist
When to seek professional help: lasting weeks, affecting sleep, health or work, or relying on alcohol or drugs
Thoughts of self-harm need help at once: do not leave the person alone; tell the counsellor; emergency services or hospital if in danger

essays.stem: Describe how you would make and review a personal stress management action plan.
essays.modelAnswer: First, I would find out what causes my stress by keeping a stress diary for one or two weeks, writing down when I felt stressed, what caused it, how I felt and what I did. From the diary I would pick my main causes, for example falling behind with practical work and the cost of travel to the Centre. For each cause I would write a SMART goal and the steps to reach it, such as planning my week with a to-do list, asking my instructor for extra help with room preparation, and making a simple budget for travel and lunch. I would add healthy habits to my plan, such as walking three times a week, going to bed by a set time, drinking enough water and cutting down on energy drinks. I would write down the early signs that show my stress is rising, and who I can talk to for support, including the Centre's counsellor. After two to four weeks, I would review the plan: check which steps helped and which did not, and change the plan where needed. I would keep reviewing it regularly.
markingPoints: Uses a stress diary to find the causes
Picks the main causes and sets SMART goals and steps for each
Includes healthy habits
Notes early warning signs and who can give support
Reviews the plan after a set time and changes it where needed

practical1.title: Make a stress-awareness poster and give a short talk for hotel and villa staff
practical1.brief: As a group, plan, make and present a stress-awareness poster for a hotel or villa staff room, then use it to give a 10-minute talk to the assessor and another group, as you would at a staff briefing. The poster must show: what stress is; common causes in hotels, villas and kitchens (such as heavy workloads before check-in, long shifts, the busy season and difficult guests); physical, emotional and behaviour signs; why stress is a safety risk around knives, hot oil, chemicals and lifting; at least four healthy ways to cope; and where trainees and staff can get help, including the Centre's own support contacts. Share the work so that each member researches and writes one section and presents it in the talk. Use your own words and drawings. Collect written feedback from at least two listeners on a simple feedback form, and note one change you would make. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the poster, the planning notes and the feedback forms once for the whole group.
materials: Chart paper or a large card, markers, rulers and glue
Paper and pens for planning notes
Information sheets from the instructor on stress, with the Centre's support contacts
photos: The group's planning notes, showing who is doing each section
The talk, with each member presenting their section
The completed feedback forms and the group's note on one change
checklist: Took part in planning and agreed their section with the group
Wrote their section in their own clear words, and it was correct
Included correct signs, causes or coping methods for their section
Linked stress to safety or guest service where it fitted their section
Presented their section clearly and answered a question about it
Listened to others and helped collect and act on the feedback
safety: Use scissors and craft knives carefully, and keep the work area tidy
Do not put any member's private or personal details on the poster
If any member is upset by the topic, they can step out and talk to the instructor or the Centre's counsellor
If the poster is put up, fix it securely where it does not block a door or walkway

practical2.title: Role play: handling stress at a hotel, then write a stress action plan
practical2.brief: As a group, act out three short workplace scenes given by the assessor, for example: a room attendant with more rooms than she can finish before check-in speaking to the supervisor; a front desk agent staying calm with an angry guest whose room is not ready, then talking it through with a co-worker afterwards; and a cook noticing that a co-worker seems very stressed and offering support, including where to get help. Each member plays a part in at least one scene and observes at least one other, filling in an observation sheet on what went well and what could be better. After each scene, the group discusses it and writes down the main points. Then each member writes a stress action plan, covering causes, early signs, SMART goals and steps, healthy habits and who can give support. A member may write the plan for a made-up worker if they prefer not to share personal details. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and the written sheets to the group's practical.
materials: Three scene cards from the assessor
Observation sheets, one for each member
Blank stress action plan forms, one for each member
A desk and chair set up as a front desk, pens and clipboards
A list of the Centre's support contacts
photos: The group reading the scene cards and choosing roles
The group's notes from the discussion after the scenes
Each member's completed stress action plan (personal details covered if wanted)
checklist: Played their part in a scene clearly, staying calm, polite and assertive
Used good listening and "I" statements where the scene needed it
Suggested a sensible solution or source of help in their scene
Completed an observation sheet with useful comments
Took part in the group discussion after each scene
Completed a stress action plan with causes, signs, SMART goals, healthy habits and support
safety: Keep the role plays calm: no real shouting, pushing or touching
Treat each other with respect; nobody is forced to share private matters
Any member who becomes upset can stop and speak privately with the instructor or the Centre's counsellor
Keep the room tidy so that nobody trips while moving between scenes
